name: Tesamorelin

b.x: Eighteen percent less visceral fat at six months. That's the headline number from the first of two double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 3 trials, which together randomized 816 participants. The second trial landed at 14% (EGRIFTA SV label, section 14). The tesamorelin peptide (trade name Egrifta SV, also marketed as Egrifta WR, compound code TH9507 (CAS 218949-48-5)) is a synthetic 44-amino-acid GHRH analog with an added trans-3-hexenoic acid modification that extends stability beyond native GHRH. The mechanism is straightforward. Tesamorelin binds the GHRH receptor on anterior pituitary somatotrophs, producing pulsatile GH release rather than flat tonic elevation. That GH pulse drives hepatic IGF-1 production, and IGF-1 mediates the downstream lipolysis, targeting visceral adipose depots. Subcutaneous bioavailability runs below 4% per the FDA label (Section 12.3), yet the receptor-level response is potent enough to produce measurable body composition changes. In clinical practice, the FDA approved tesamorelin in 2010 for HIV-associated lipodystrophy with excess visceral adipose tissue. Falutz and colleagues published the second trial on its own in 2010 (n=404) [1]. Visceral fat fell 10.9% (21 cm squared) at six months, versus a 0.6% drop on placebo. Patients who stayed on tesamorelin reached about 18% at 12 months. A pooled analysis of both trials (806 patients) [6] put the 26-week treatment effect at 15.4%. Beyond HIV, the off-label use has expanded considerably. Stanley and colleagues published a 2019 Lancet HIV trial [2] showing 35% of patients achieved liver fat below 5% at 12 months, establishing a potential NAFLD benefit. Baker et al. [3] demonstrated improved executive function in older adults and MCI patients after 20 weeks of GHRH treatment in a 152-person RCT. Community dosing follows the 2 mg daily Phase 3 trial dose, injected subcutaneously into the abdomen, with most protocols running 12 to 26 weeks followed by a rest period. The current EGRIFTA SV label dose is 1.4 mg daily. Sermorelin was discontinued by EMD Serono in 2008, and FDA withdrew its approval in 2009, not for safety or effectiveness reasons. That leaves tesamorelin with the only active FDA approval among GHRH analogs. Both clear fast, with label half-lives of 8 to 11 minutes for tesamorelin and 11 to 12 minutes for sermorelin.

Tesamorelin binds the growth hormone releasing hormone receptor (GHRH-R) on anterior pituitary somatotroph cells. Tesamorelin is a modified analog of endogenous GHRH(1-44)NH2 with a trans-3-hexenoic acid group attached to the tyrosine at position 1. That chemical modification protects against enzymatic degradation, but clearance is still fast. The current EGRIFTA labels (section 12.3) list a mean half-life of 8 minutes for SV and 11 minutes for WR after one subcutaneous dose. Once GHRH-R activates, the intracellular signaling cascade mirrors what happens with natural GHRH. Cyclic AMP rises in somatotrophs, calcium channels open, and GH vesicles release into the bloodstream. The resulting GH pulse peaks quickly; Tmax occurs at approximately 9 minutes post-injection. GH then stimulates hepatic IGF-1 synthesis. IGF-1 is the workhorse molecule for tissue-level effects: lipolysis in visceral adipose, protein synthesis in muscle, collagen turnover, and hepatic fat metabolism. The visceral fat selectivity is a GH-pathway feature, not a tesamorelin-specific property. GH-driven lipolysis preferentially targets visceral adipose tissue because visceral fat cells express higher densities of GH receptors and beta-adrenergic receptors than subcutaneous fat. The two Phase 3 trials fit this pattern: visceral fat dropped 14 to 18% while abdominal subcutaneous fat showed no significant change [6]. Because tesamorelin works through the pituitary, the hypothalamic feedback loop stays intact. Somatostatin is the natural brake on GH secretion. This self-regulating mechanism is why tesamorelin produces physiological pulsatile GH release rather than the flat supraphysiological elevation seen with exogenous HGH.
Tesamorelin benefits center on FDA-validated visceral fat reduction and GH axis activation through the most potent available GHRH analog.

Visceral fat fell 18% and 14% at 26 weeks in two double-blind Phase 3 trials of 816 patients. Waist circumference dropped 1 to 2 cm more than on placebo (EGRIFTA SV label, section 14). Pooled, the treatment effect on visceral fat was 15.4% [6].
Liver fat cleared below 5% in 35% of patients at 12 months in Stanley et al.'s Lancet HIV RCT [2], with fibrosis progression significantly slowed across the trial.
Cognitive function improved in a 152-person RCT (Baker et al. 2012) [3], showing better executive function and working memory in older adults and MCI patients after 20 weeks of GHRH treatment.
IGF-1 typically rises 50 to 100% above baseline within four to six weeks, confirming GH axis activation and serving as a practical biomarker for peptide quality and injection technique.

Sleep quality and recovery improvements within the first two weeks are among the most consistently reported early effects across community threads, preceding visible body composition changes by several weeks.

Metabolic panel improvements, including triglyceride reduction and better lipid profiles, tracked in Phase 3 trial secondary endpoints and confirmed by off-label users monitoring bloodwork during 12 to 26 week cycles.
Aligned
Scientific Evidence
Based on 21 key studies · FDA-approved
FDA-approved GHRH analog with strong Phase 3 RCT data (n=816 randomized across two trials).

Dosing studied: 1.4 mg once daily SC abdomen (EGRIFTA SV label); EGRIFTA WR 1.28 mg once daily, not substitutable; the Phase 3 trials used 2 mg with the original 1 mg-vial EGRIFTA; community off-label uses 1–2 mg/day

VAT fell 18% and 14% at 26 weeks versus +2% and −2% on placebo (label section 14); the pooled treatment effect was −15.4% [6]. NAFLD benefit in HIV shown in Lancet HIV 2019 RCT (35% achieved liver fat <5% at 12 months). Cognitive benefit (executive function in MCI and healthy older adults) shown in 2012 RCT (n=152). 2024 INSTI-era study (n=61) [4] confirmed efficacy persists on modern ART regimens with no exacerbation of glycemic control. Active Phase 2 trial (TRIUMPH, NCT06554717) exploring exercise adjunct in HIV. Mechanism well-established: GHRH analog → pulsatile GH release → IGF-1 rise → visceral lipolysis. SC bioavailability <4% but potent at receptor level.
Key Study

Falutz et al. 2010, J Clin Endocrinol Metab (PMID 20554713): pooled analysis of both Phase 3 trials (n=806), 26 weeks: VAT −24 vs. +2 cm² placebo, treatment effect −15.4%; −17.5% at 52 weeks with continued use. Falutz et al. 2010, JAIDS (PMID 20101189): the second trial alone (n=404), VAT −10.9% vs. −0.6% placebo at 26 weeks. Stanley et al. 2019 (PMID 31611038) Lancet HIV for NAFLD indication.
Limitations

FDA approval limited to HIV-associated lipodystrophy; off-label use for general visceral fat reduction or cognition lacks large RCTs in non-HIV populations. SC bioavailability <4% means batch-to-batch potency variation in compounded product is clinically meaningful. Anti-tesamorelin antibodies in ~50% of patients (10% neutralizing in vitro at week 52), with comparable VAT and IGF-1 changes with or without them (label section 12.6). IGF-1 monitoring burden. No data in large non-HIV populations.
Community Experience
Regarded as the most targeted visceral fat peptide available.
Community dosing: 1–2 mg/day SC abdomen; most use 2 mg/day, the Phase 3 trial dose; some beginners use 1 mg/day to assess tolerance

Community broadly follows the 2 mg/day Phase 3 trial dose (SC abdomen), above the 1.4 mg EGRIFTA SV label dose. Off-label use well-established among non-HIV users for belly fat reduction and GH optimization. Strong overlap between clinical expectations and community-reported outcomes. Primary criticisms: cost of compounded product, abdominal-only injection requirement, and IGF-1 testing burden.
What users report (5)
Visible reduction in abdominal visceral fat by weeks 8–12
Waist circumference measurably decreases by month 3
Improved sleep quality and body recomposition alongside fat loss
Better metabolic markers (triglycerides, lipid profile) in some users
Cognitive clarity and improved focus reported by users stacking for GH optimization
Common issues (5)
High cost of compounded product ($150–$300/month) limits long-term use
Abdominal-only injection requirement (per FDA label) limits site rotation options
Joint pain and water retention in first 2–4 weeks
Glucose increases monitored by users, especially those with metabolic syndrome
Antibody formation over extended cycles may blunt response
Science & Community Aligned

Community dosing mirrors the 2 mg/day Phase 3 trial dose; the current EGRIFTA SV label dose is 1.4 mg/day. Reported outcomes for visceral fat reduction closely match the Phase 3 trial data. Off-label cognitive and GH optimization uses are an extension of the clinical mechanism, not a contradiction. Main divergence: community runs 3–6 month cycles with breaks whereas the FDA label supports ongoing continuous treatment.

FDA Label EGRIFTA SV (tesamorelin) FDA Prescribing Information (2026): 1.4 mg once daily (n=816 (two Phase 3 trials)) [Source](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=3d783378-b02d-4f19-99dd-0fc91a042224)

With a 5 mg vial and 2 mL bacteriostatic water, you get 2.5 mg/mL (2500 mcg/mL). At that concentration: 2000 mcg (the 2 mg Phase 3 trial dose most community protocols use) is 80 units on a U-100 insulin syringe. That's 0.8 mL, so you'll use close to half the syringe. Each 5 mg vial gives you 2.5 daily doses at 2 mg per day. The EGRIFTA SV label dose is lower: 1.4 mg (0.35 mL of its own reconstituted 2 mg vial) once daily. With the 2 mg vial (EGRIFTA SV) and 0.5 mL of diluent, you get 4 mg/mL: 1.4 mg is 35 units (0.35 mL), and a 2 mg dose is the whole vial, 50 units (0.5 mL). Each 2 mg vial makes one dose. Inject into abdominal subcutaneous fat only. The FDA label specifies this, and the clinical data was collected this way. Don't rotate to thigh or arm. Rotate within the abdomen, at least 2 cm from the umbilicus. The non-obvious thing: your IGF-1 check at four to six weeks isn't optional. If IGF-1 hasn't risen, either the peptide is degraded, your injection technique is off, or you've drawn a bad batch from the compounder. Don't run a full 26-week cycle without confirming the molecule is actually working. Pre-bed injection is the community preference for off-label use because it matches the natural nocturnal GH surge. FDA trials used morning dosing. Either works; consistency matters more than timing.
Tesamorelin Cycle

Cycling here is a community practice, not a label instruction. The FDA label supports ongoing treatment, and its immunogenicity data give no antibody reason to stop (EGRIFTA SV label, section 12.6). About 50% of patients formed anti-tesamorelin antibodies and 10% had neutralizing antibodies at week 52, with comparable VAT and IGF-1 changes either way. Community and clinic protocols add 4 to 8 week rest periods for cost, adherence, a pause in IGF-1 elevation and structured glucose checks. The trade-off is regain; VAT came back within six months of stopping in both trials (section 14).

You'll need a 2 mg tesamorelin vial (lyophilized powder), 0.5 mL of diluent, a mixing syringe with an 18-gauge needle for reconstitution, and a U-100 insulin syringe (29 to 31 gauge, half-inch needle) for injection. EGRIFTA SV comes with its own diluent, and its label says to use only that one. Do not use bacteriostatic water with EGRIFTA SV. For a compounded vial, use the diluent your pharmacy names.

Draw 0.5 mL of diluent into the mixing syringe. Inject slowly down the inside wall of the vial. Do not shake; roll the vial gently between your hands until the powder dissolves. This gives you 4 mg/mL. The solution should be clear and colorless; discard if cloudy or discolored.
Using a fresh U-100 insulin syringe, draw 35 units (0.35 mL) for the 1.4 mg EGRIFTA SV label dose. The 2 mg Phase 3 trial dose most community protocols use is 50 units (0.5 mL, the whole vial).
Abdominal subcutaneous fat, at least 2 cm away from your navel. Avoid scar tissue and bruised areas. Rotate sites with each injection to prevent localized lipoatrophy.

Inject EGRIFTA SV right after mixing, then throw away what's left in the vial and the diluent bottle. Its label says not to refrigerate or freeze a mixed vial. For compounded vials, follow your pharmacy's storage directions.
Pre-bed works well for off-label use (matches nocturnal GH pulse). Morning dosing was used in FDA trials. Pick one time and stay consistent.

Works With
Ipamorelin

Classic GHRH + GHRP dual-pathway stack. Tesamorelin provides the GHRH signal; ipamorelin provides the GHRP pulse: community protocols co-administer them for a larger combined GH release. Ipamorelin is the preferred GHRP for its clean profile. In swine it raised GH without raising cortisol or prolactin (PMID 9849822), and users report little hunger.
Inject both simultaneously or within 5 minutes. Tesamorelin 2000 mcg + ipamorelin 200–300 mcg, once daily SC abdomen.
GHRP-2

Alternative GHRP. In swine, GHRP-2 released GH at a lower dose than ipamorelin (ED50 0.6 vs 2.3 nmol/kg) but reached a lower peak (56 vs 65 ng/mL; Raun 1998, PMID 9849822). In people it modestly raises cortisol and prolactin (Arvat 1997, PMID 9285939). Used when cortisol co-stimulation is acceptable.
Tesamorelin 2000 mcg + GHRP-2 100–200 mcg, once daily pre-bed SC abdomen.
Hexarelin

Most potent GHRP available; produces the largest GH pulse per injection. Combined with tesamorelin for maximum GH axis activation in experienced users. Desensitization occurs faster than ipamorelin: typically cycled 4–8 weeks on, 4 weeks off.
Tesamorelin 2000 mcg + hexarelin 100–200 mcg, once daily SC abdomen. Short cycles only.
Semaglutide

GLP-1 agonist + GHRH analog for dual-mechanism fat reduction. GLP-1 addresses subcutaneous and total body fat via appetite/insulin pathway; tesamorelin targets visceral fat specifically via GH pathway. Used in some telehealth clinic protocols for significant metabolic syndrome.
Avoid
HGH (Somatropin)

Both tesamorelin and exogenous HGH elevate IGF-1. Combination risks supraphysiological IGF-1 levels, worsened insulin resistance, peripheral edema, and acromegaly-like effects with prolonged use. No clinical or community rationale for combining: choose one GH pathway strategy.
MK-677 (Ibutamoren)

Both significantly raise GH and IGF-1 through complementary mechanisms (GHRH vs. ghrelin receptor). Combination produces excessive IGF-1 elevation and compounded insulin resistance risk. Glucose and metabolic effects are additive. Use one at a time.
CJC-1295 (with DAC)

Both are GHRH analogs: redundant mechanism. Both occupy GHRH receptors and produce pulsatile GH release. Combining two GHRH analogs does not increase efficacy and may cause receptor saturation and unnecessary IGF-1 burden.

Egrifta SV: ~$3,085/month (typical US cash price without insurance, 2026); Egrifta WR: ~$41,000/year list price. Patient assistance programs exist for qualifying patients.

Glucose management is the most important safety concern with tesamorelin. GH-mediated insulin resistance is a class effect of all GHRH analogs, and the FDA label includes specific warnings about new-onset diabetes and glucose intolerance. Fasting glucose and HbA1c must be monitored at baseline, then every three to six months during treatment. A fasting glucose above 126 mg/dL or HbA1c above 6.5% means stopping or significantly adjusting the protocol. Pre-diabetic users and those with metabolic syndrome carry higher risk. The 2024 INSTI-era study (n=61) [4] confirmed that tesamorelin on modern ART regimens did not exacerbate glycemic control, but that data applies to the HIV population specifically. Active malignancy is an absolute contraindication. Tesamorelin raises IGF-1, and IGF-1 promotes cell proliferation. The FDA label explicitly contraindicates use in patients with active or recurrent cancer. Newly diagnosed malignancy during treatment requires immediate discontinuation. This is not a theoretical concern; it's a black-box-level warning. Anti-tesamorelin IgG antibodies showed up in 50% of trial patients at 26 weeks and 47% at 52 weeks (EGRIFTA SV label, section 12.6). Visceral fat and IGF-1 responses were similar with or without them. Neutralizing antibodies turned up in vitro in 10% by week 52, and changes in that group were comparable too. Antibodies were far more common in people with hypersensitivity reactions, at 85% of that subset. Community protocols often add 4 to 8 week breaks; the label data give no antibody reason for them. Injection site reactions are common in the first week: redness, pain, and induration at the abdominal injection site. The FDA label specifies abdominal subcutaneous injection only for this indication. Repeated injection into the same small area can cause localized lipoatrophy (skin dimpling) because tesamorelin triggers local lipolysis. Systematic site rotation across the abdomen prevents this. Avoid the area within 2 cm of the umbilicus and any scarred or bruised skin. Joint pain and peripheral edema affect some users in the first two to four weeks as IGF-1 rises and fluid retention increases. Community reports describe this as self-resolving in most cases. If symptoms persist beyond four weeks, reducing the dose to 1 mg per day usually resolves them. NSAIDs help short-term for joint pain; leg elevation helps for lower extremity edema. Pregnancy is contraindicated due to potential fetal harm per the FDA label. Breastfeeding lacks sufficient safety data. Patients with disruption of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis from hypophysectomy, pituitary tumor, or pituitary surgery should not use tesamorelin, as the mechanism requires functional pituitary somatotrophs. Known hypersensitivity to tesamorelin or mannitol (used as an excipient in the formulation) is a contraindication. When to see a doctor: persistent edema beyond four weeks, fasting glucose above 126 mg/dL, joint pain unresponsive to dose reduction, any new or worsening mass or tumor, or signs of glucose intolerance.
Common Issues & Solutions

No measurable VAT reduction by week 8–10: verify injection technique (SC, not IM; rotate abdominal sites), confirm IGF-1 has risen from baseline at 4-week check. If IGF-1 not rising, suspect reconstitution error or inactive/degraded peptide; in the trials, IGF-1 rose similarly with or without anti-tesamorelin antibodies (label section 12.6).

Injection site lipoatrophy or skin dimpling: rotate sites systematically across the abdomen; avoid repeated injection into the same 1 cm area. Tesamorelin causes local lipolysis: a known effect that reverses when sites are properly rotated.

Fasting glucose rising: expected GH-mediated insulin resistance: must be monitored. At first sign of glucose rise >10 mg/dL from baseline, add quarterly HbA1c monitoring. In pre-diabetic users, consider dose reduction to 1 mg/day or discontinuation.

Response diminishing after initial benefit (months 3–6+): the label data do not support antibodies as the cause. ~50% of trial patients formed them and 10% had neutralizing antibodies by week 52, yet VAT and IGF-1 changes were comparable (label section 12.6). Recheck IGF-1, injection technique and product quality first.

Joint pain, stiffness, or peripheral edema: common in first 2–4 weeks as IGF-1 rises and fluid retention increases. Usually self-resolving. If persistent beyond 4 weeks or severe, reduce dose to 1 mg/day. Elevate legs for edema; NSAIDs for joint pain short-term.

Tesamorelin: Product Quality medium risk

Tesamorelin is an FDA-approved molecule (Egrifta SV, Egrifta WR) but most off-label community use is via compounded versions, not commercially manufactured Egrifta. Compounded peptides vary in purity, concentration accuracy, and sterility. SC bioavailability <4% means potency is highly sensitive to peptide integrity; degradation or incorrect concentration directly impacts dosing. FDA has taken enforcement action against compounding pharmacies for peptides in general (2024 503A bulk list enforcement activity). A COA from the compounding pharmacy is the main quality record for a compounded batch.

Egrifta (tesamorelin) is on FDA's list of NDAs deemed to be biologics licenses on March 23, 2020, and FDA's notice to compounders says these transitioning biological products are not eligible for the 503A or 503B compounding exemptions. Unregulated research-chemical products have no oversight
A useful certificate of analysis (COA) shows HPLC purity ≥98% and mass spec identity confirmation

If IGF-1 does not rise at 4-week check despite correct reconstitution and injection technique, suspect inactive peptide: contact provider

Tesamorelin is FDA-approved (BLA 022505, an NDA until FDA deemed it a BLA on March 23, 2020) under the brand name Egrifta for the reduction of excess abdominal fat in HIV-infected patients with lipodystrophy. The original approval came in November 2010; the current EGRIFTA SV and EGRIFTA WR labels are dated July 29, 2026. This is one of a very small number of peptides with full FDA approval, Phase 3 RCT data, and an active commercial product. Commercially manufactured Egrifta SV and Egrifta WR are available through specialty pharmacies with a prescription. Brand pricing runs approximately $3,085 per month as a typical US cash price without insurance, or roughly $41,000 per year list price. Patient assistance programs exist for qualifying patients. Off-label use for general visceral fat reduction, body recomposition, or cognitive support requires a prescription from a licensed provider. Most off-label users get tesamorelin as a compounded formulation, typically at $150 to $300 per month. The FDA took enforcement actions against compounding pharmacies for peptides broadly in 2024. Egrifta is on FDA's list of applications deemed to be biologics licenses on March 23, 2020. FDA's notice to compounders says these transitioning biological products are not eligible for the 503A and 503B compounding exemptions. Tesamorelin also appears in none of FDA's 503A or 503B nomination categories (May 14, 2026; March 21, 2025). WADA prohibits all growth hormone releasing factors including tesamorelin for competitive athletes. This content is for informational purposes only. It does not constitute medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment recommendations. Consult a qualified healthcare provider before using any peptide.

faqs.q: What is the recommended tesamorelin dosage?
faqs.a: The EGRIFTA SV label dose is 1.4 mg (0.35 mL of the reconstituted 2 mg vial) injected subcutaneously once daily. EGRIFTA WR, a separate formulation, is 1.28 mg (0.16 mL) once daily, and the two are not substitutable. Both are flat doses with no titration. The Phase 3 trials used 2 mg daily with the original 1 mg-vial EGRIFTA. Community protocols sometimes use 1 mg daily for cost reasons, though efficacy data at that dose is limited.

faqs.q: What are the side effects of tesamorelin?
faqs.a: Injection site reactions (erythema, pruritus) affect about 8% of users. Joint pain (arthralgia) occurs in roughly 13% per the Egrifta label. IGF-1 elevation is expected and requires monitoring. About 50% of patients develop anti-tesamorelin antibodies during treatment; most are non-neutralizing.

faqs.q: How does tesamorelin reduce belly fat?
faqs.a: Tesamorelin is a 44-amino-acid GHRH analog that stimulates pituitary GH release. The increased GH drives lipolysis specifically in visceral adipose tissue. Two Phase 3 trials in 816 HIV-lipodystrophy patients showed 18% and 14% visceral fat reductions at 26 weeks (EGRIFTA SV label, section 14). The mechanism is GH-mediated, not appetite suppression.

Yes. Egrifta (tesamorelin) received FDA approval in 2010 for reduction of excess abdominal fat in HIV-infected patients with lipodystrophy. It is the only GHRH analog with an active FDA approval. Off-label use for non-HIV visceral fat reduction is common in anti-aging clinics.

faqs.q: How long does tesamorelin take to work?
faqs.a: The Phase 3 trials measured visceral fat reduction at 26 weeks. Measurable reductions via DEXA or CT scan typically appear around 8-12 weeks. Subjective improvements in abdominal firmness are often reported by week 4-6. VAT rebounds if treatment stops without lifestyle changes.

Tesamorelin typically comes in 2mg or 5mg vials. Add 0.5mL of the diluent its directions name to the vial. Use the free calculator for exact syringe units based on your desired dose. EGRIFTA WR is a separate kit. Its 11.6 mg vial is mixed with 1.3 mL of the supplied bacteriostatic water for 8 mg/mL, and each 1.28 mg daily dose is 0.16 mL (EGRIFTA WR label, section 2.2). Vial math does not give those numbers, so the calculator is set up for EGRIFTA SV.

faqs.q: What is the half-life of Tesamorelin?
faqs.a: The half-life of Tesamorelin is 8-11 min (single SC dose, EGRIFTA SV and WR labels). This determines how frequently you need to dose for consistent blood levels.

summary: Visceral fat fell 14 to 18% in 26 weeks across two Phase 3 trials that randomized 816 patients (EGRIFTA SV label, section 14). The tesamorelin peptide (Egrifta) is an FDA-approved GHRH analog that triggers pulsatile GH release, targeting visceral adipose tissue. Subcutaneous bioavailability sits below 4%, yet receptor-level potency still produces reliable IGF-1 elevation and consistent abdominal fat loss. The gains need ongoing use; visceral fat came back within six months of stopping in both trials. About half of trial patients formed anti-tesamorelin antibodies, but visceral fat and IGF-1 changes were similar with or without them (section 12.6). Adults with stubborn visceral belly fat, HIV lipodystrophy patients, and those pursuing GH optimization through the most potent available GHRH analog are the primary users.
